Learning Rate Limits: How Eigenvalues Decide Whether an AI Model Learns or Explodes¶

25BSMA01 Matrix Algebra and Calculus · Experiential Learning · Jain University (FET)

We train the simplest possible "AI model" — a linear regression that predicts Bengaluru house prices from area and number of bedrooms — and show that matrix algebra and calculus predict exactly when training works and when it explodes.

Part Topic Syllabus
1 Data & the system of equations (rank, consistency) Module I · CO1
2 Solving it: Gauss elimination vs Gauss-Seidel / Jacobi Module I · CO1
3 The loss surface: partial derivatives, maxima/minima, eigenvalues Module III · CO3

6 The learning-rate limit Modules I + II · CO6

Part 1 — Data & the system of equations¶

Syllabus link: Module I — systems of linear equations, rank, consistency (CO1)

What we compute: the matrix $A$ and vector $b$ of the normal equations $A\,w = b$, and the rank test that tells us whether the system has a unique solution.

Key result: $\operatorname{rank}(A) = \operatorname{rank}([A\,|\,b]) = 2$ = number of unknowns $\Rightarrow$ exactly one best set of weights.

1.1 Load the data¶

9,858 cleaned listings from the Kaggle Bengaluru House Price Data set. Price is in ₹ lakhs (1 lakh = ₹1,00,000).

1.2 Standardise the data¶

Each column is rescaled to mean 0 and standard deviation 1 (population std, i.e. divide by $n$):

$$z = \frac{x - \bar{x}}{\sigma}$$

Because every column now has mean 0, the best-fit line passes through the origin, so the intercept is exactly 0 and the model has only two weights $w = (w_1, w_2)$:

$$\hat{t} = w_1 z_{\text{sqft}} + w_2 z_{\text{bhk}}$$

In [5]:
columns = ["sqft", "bhk", "price_lakhs"]
means = houses[columns].mean()
stds = houses[columns].std(ddof=0)          # population standard deviation (divide by n)
standardised = (houses[columns] - means) / stds

Z = standardised[["sqft", "bhk"]].to_numpy()   # n x 2 feature matrix
t = standardised["price_lakhs"].to_numpy()     # n target values

print("Means:              ", means.round(3).to_dict())
print("Standard deviations:", stds.round(3).to_dict())
print("After standardising, means ≈", standardised.mean().round(10).to_dict())
print("After standardising, stds  =", standardised.std(ddof=0).round(10).to_dict())

results["n_rows"] = n
results["means"] = means.to_dict()
results["stds"] = stds.to_dict()

1.3 The loss and the normal equations¶

We measure how wrong the model is with the mean squared error (with a convenient factor ½):

$$L(w) = \frac{1}{2n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(z_i \cdot w - t_i\right)^2$$

Setting the gradient to zero (Part 3 derives this) gives a non-homogeneous linear system, the normal equations:

$$A\,w = b, \qquad A = \frac{Z^{\mathsf T}Z}{n}, \qquad b = \frac{Z^{\mathsf T}t}{n}$$

For standardised data $A$ is the correlation matrix $\begin{pmatrix}1 & \rho\\ \rho & 1\end{pmatrix}$ and $b$ holds the correlations of each feature with price.

In [6]:
# Module I: build the coefficient matrix A and right-hand side b of the normal equations

b = Z.T @ t / n

print("b =", b)

print(houses[columns].corr().round(4))

results["A"] = A
results["b"] = b

1.4 Rank and consistency¶

For a non-homogeneous system $A\,w = b$ with $k$ unknowns:

  • $\operatorname{rank}(A) \ne \operatorname{rank}([A\,|\,b])$ → inconsistent (no solution)
  • $\operatorname{rank}(A) = \operatorname{rank}([A\,|\,b]) = k$ → unique solution
  • $\operatorname{rank}(A) = \operatorname{rank}([A\,|\,b]) < k$ → infinitely many solutions

We find the rank by row-reducing to echelon form and counting the non-zero rows.

In [7]:
def rank_by_row_reduction(M, tol=1e-10):
    """Module I: rank = number of non-zero rows after reducing M to echelon form."""
    M = np.array(M, dtype=float)
    rows, cols = M.shape
    rank = 0
    for col in range(cols):
        if rank == rows:
            break
        # choose the row (at or below the current one) with the largest entry in this column
        pivot_row = rank + np.argmax(np.abs(M[rank:, col]))
        if abs(M[pivot_row, col]) < tol:
            continue                                   # no pivot in this column
        M[[rank, pivot_row]] = M[[pivot_row, rank]]    # swap rows
        for r in range(rank + 1, rows):                # eliminate entries below the pivot
            M[r] -= (M[r, col] / M[rank, col]) * M[rank]
        rank += 1
    return rank

augmented = np.column_stack([A, b])                    # [A | b]
rank_A = rank_by_row_reduction(A)
rank_aug = rank_by_row_reduction(augmented)

print(f"rank(A)     = {rank_A}   (numpy check: {np.linalg.matrix_rank(A)})")
print(f"rank([A|b]) = {rank_aug}   (numpy check: {np.linalg.matrix_rank(augmented)})")
print("Number of unknowns k = 2")
if rank_A == rank_aug == 2:
    print("=> Consistent, rank = k  =>  UNIQUE solution w*")

results["rank_A"] = rank_A
results["rank_augmented"] = rank_aug

rank(A)     = 2   (numpy check: 2)
rank([A|b]) = 2   (numpy check: 2)

1.5 What if we add duplicate information? (rank-deficient demo)¶

Add a third feature: the same area measured in square metres, $\text{sqft\_m2} = 0.092903 \times \text{sqft}$. After standardising it is identical to the sqft column, so the $3 \times 3$ matrix $A_3$ has two equal rows.

In [8]:
houses_3 = houses.copy()
houses_3["sqft_m2"] = houses_3["sqft"] * 0.092903

features_3 = ["sqft", "bhk", "sqft_m2"]
Z3 = ((houses_3[features_3] - houses_3[features_3].mean()) / houses_3[features_3].std(ddof=0)).to_numpy()

A3 = Z3.T @ Z3 / n
b3 = Z3.T @ t / n
augmented3 = np.column_stack([A3, b3])

rank_A3 = rank_by_row_reduction(A3)
rank_aug3 = rank_by_row_reduction(augmented3)
eigs_A3 = np.linalg.eigvalsh(A3)
eigs_A3[np.abs(eigs_A3) < 1e-10] = 0.0         # tiny round-off (~1e-16) is really zero

print("A3 =\n", A3)
print("b3 =", b3)
print(f"rank(A3)      = {rank_A3}   (numpy check: {np.linalg.matrix_rank(A3)})")
print(f"rank([A3|b3]) = {rank_aug3}   (numpy check: {np.linalg.matrix_rank(augmented3)})")

In one line: duplicate information (the same area in two units) makes the model's answer non-unique — the weight can be split between sqft and sqft_m2 in infinitely many ways.

Part 2 — Solving it: Gauss elimination vs Gauss-Seidel¶

Syllabus link: Module I — Gauss elimination (direct method), Gauss-Seidel and Jacobi (iterative methods) (CO1)

What we compute: the best weights $w^*$ by a direct method, then by two iterative methods, and compare how fast the iterative methods converge.

Key result: $w^* = (0.9645,\ -0.1592)$. Gauss-Seidel needs 24 iterations, Jacobi 56.

2.1 Gauss elimination¶

Forward elimination: use row operations $R_2 \to R_2 - \frac{a_{21}}{a_{11}} R_1$ on the augmented matrix $[A\,|\,b]$ to reach echelon (upper-triangular) form. Back-substitution: solve the last equation first, then work upwards.

In [9]:
def gauss_elimination(A, b):
    """Module I: Gauss elimination. Returns the echelon form of [A|b] and the solution."""
    M = np.column_stack([A, b]).astype(float)       # augmented matrix [A | b]
    k = len(b)

    # Module I: Gauss elimination – forward elimination step
    for pivot in range(k):
        for row in range(pivot + 1, k):
            multiplier = M[row, pivot] / M[pivot, pivot]
            M[row] = M[row] - multiplier * M[pivot]       # R_row -> R_row - m * R_pivot

    # Module I: Gauss elimination – back-substitution step
    x = np.zeros(k)
    for row in range(k - 1, -1, -1):
        known = sum(M[row, col] * x[col] for col in range(row + 1, k))
        x[row] = (M[row, k] - known) / M[row, row]
    return M, x

echelon, w_star = gauss_elimination(A, b)
w_star_numpy = np.linalg.solve(A, b)

print("Echelon form of [A | b]:\n", echelon)
print(f"Gauss elimination:  w* = ({w_star[0]:.4f}, {w_star[1]:.4f})")
print(f"numpy check:        w* = ({w_star_numpy[0]:.4f}, {w_star_numpy[1]:.4f})")

results["echelon_form"] = echelon
results["w_star"] = w_star
results["w_star_numpy_check"] = w_star_numpy

2.2 Gauss-Seidel and Jacobi iteration¶

Rewrite each equation to make one unknown the subject:

$$w_1 = \frac{b_1 - \rho\, w_2}{1}, \qquad w_2 = \frac{b_2 - \rho\, w_1}{1}$$

  • Jacobi uses only the old values from the previous iteration.
  • Gauss-Seidel uses the newest value of $w_1$ straight away when computing $w_2$ — so it is faster.

Start from $w = (0, 0)$; stop when the largest change between iterations is below $10^{-6}$.

Convergence guarantee: $A$ is strictly diagonally dominant ($|1| > |\rho|$ in every row), so both methods are guaranteed to converge.

In [10]:
TOLERANCE = 1e-6

def is_diagonally_dominant(A):
    """Each diagonal entry is bigger (in size) than the sum of the other entries in its row."""
    return all(abs(A[i, i]) > sum(abs(A[i, j]) for j in range(len(A)) if j != i) for i in range(len(A)))

def gauss_seidel(A, b, tol=TOLERANCE, max_iter=1000):
    """Module I: Gauss-Seidel – each new value is used immediately."""
    x = np.zeros(len(b))
    history = [x.copy()]
    for _ in range(max_iter):
        old = x.copy()
        for i in range(len(b)):
            others = sum(A[i, j] * x[j] for j in range(len(b)) if j != i)   # newest values
            x[i] = (b[i] - others) / A[i, i]
        history.append(x.copy())
        if np.max(np.abs(x - old)) < tol:
            break
    return x, history

def jacobi(A, b, tol=TOLERANCE, max_iter=1000):
    """Module I: Jacobi – every new value uses only the previous iteration."""
    x = np.zeros(len(b))
    history = [x.copy()]
    for _ in range(max_iter):
        old = x.copy()
        for i in range(len(b)):
            others = sum(A[i, j] * old[j] for j in range(len(b)) if j != i)  # old values only
            x[i] = (b[i] - others) / A[i, i]
        history.append(x.copy())
        if np.max(np.abs(x - old)) < tol:
            break
    return x, history

print("A is strictly diagonally dominant:", is_diagonally_dominant(A))

w_gs, history_gs = gauss_seidel(A, b)
w_jacobi, history_jacobi = jacobi(A, b)
gs_iterations = len(history_gs) - 1          # history[0] is the starting point
jacobi_iterations = len(history_jacobi) - 1

print(f"\nGauss-Seidel: {gs_iterations} iterations -> w = ({w_gs[0]:.4f}, {w_gs[1]:.4f})")
print(f"Jacobi:       {jacobi_iterations} iterations -> w = ({w_jacobi[0]:.4f}, {w_jacobi[1]:.4f})")

Part 3 — The loss surface: partial derivatives & the minimum test¶

Syllabus link: Module III — partial derivatives, chain rule, Jacobian, maxima and minima of functions of two variables (CO3); eigenvalues via the characteristic equation (Module I)

What we compute: the gradient of the loss, the second-derivative test at $w^*$, and the eigenvalues of the Hessian, which describe the shape of the loss bowl.

Key result: $rt - s^2 = 0.3951 > 0$ and $r > 0$ → $w^*$ is a minimum. Eigenvalues $\lambda = 1 \pm \rho = 0.2223,\ 1.7777$ — a long, narrow valley (condition number ≈ 8).

3.1 The loss as a function of two variables¶

$$L(w_1, w_2) = \frac{1}{2n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(w_1 z_{i1} + w_2 z_{i2} - t_i\right)^2$$

Expanding the square and using $A$ and $b$ gives the same thing as a quadratic:

$$L(w_1, w_2) = \tfrac12\left(w_1^2 + 2\rho\, w_1 w_2 + w_2^2\right) - b_1 w_1 - b_2 w_2 + \tfrac12$$

Partial derivatives (differentiate with respect to one weight, treating the other as constant):

$$\frac{\partial L}{\partial w_1} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_i e_i\, z_{i1} = w_1 + \rho\, w_2 - b_1, \qquad \frac{\partial L}{\partial w_2} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_i e_i\, z_{i2} = \rho\, w_1 + w_2 - b_2$$

where $e_i = \hat t_i - t_i$ is the error on house $i$. In matrix form: $\nabla L = A\,w - b$.

In [14]:
def loss(w):
    """L(w) = (1/2n) * sum of squared errors."""
    errors = Z @ w - t
    return np.sum(errors ** 2) / (2 * n)

def gradient(w):
    """Module III: partial derivatives of L, written in matrix form: grad L = A w - b."""
    return A @ w - b

# Check the formula against finite differences at a test point
w_test = np.array([-1.5, -1.0])
h = 1e-6
dL_dw1_numeric = (loss(w_test + [h, 0]) - loss(w_test - [h, 0])) / (2 * h)
dL_dw2_numeric = (loss(w_test + [0, h]) - loss(w_test - [0, h])) / (2 * h)

print("At w =", w_test)
print(f"  dL/dw1: formula = {gradient(w_test)[0]:.6f}   finite difference = {dL_dw1_numeric:.6f}")
print(f"  dL/dw2: formula = {gradient(w_test)[1]:.6f}   finite difference = {dL_dw2_numeric:.6f}")

At w = [-1.5 -1. ]
  dL/dw1: formula = -3.118428   finite difference = -3.118428
  dL/dw2: formula = -2.757576   finite difference = -2.757576

3.2 Chain rule = backpropagation¶

The loss depends on the weights only through a chain of steps:

$$w \;\longrightarrow\; \hat t_i = z_i \cdot w \;\longrightarrow\; e_i = \hat t_i - t_i \;\longrightarrow\; L = \frac{1}{2n}\sum e_i^2$$

The chain rule multiplies the local derivatives along this chain:

$$\frac{\partial L}{\partial w_1} = \sum_i \underbrace{\frac{\partial L}{\partial e_i}}_{e_i/n}\cdot \underbrace{\frac{\partial e_i}{\partial \hat t_i}}_{1}\cdot \underbrace{\frac{\partial \hat t_i}{\partial w_1}}_{z_{i1}} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_i e_i\, z_{i1}$$

This "multiply local derivatives backwards along the chain" is exactly what backpropagation does in every neural network. The Jacobian of the predictions with respect to the weights, $\partial \hat t / \partial w$, is simply the $n \times 2$ matrix $Z$.

In [15]:
# Module III: chain rule, computed step by step (this is backpropagation)
w = w_test
predictions = Z @ w                      # forward pass:  t_hat = Z w
errors = predictions - t                 # forward pass:  e = t_hat - t
dL_de = errors / n                       # dL/de_i  = e_i / n
de_dprediction = np.ones(n)              # de_i/dt_hat_i = 1
jacobian = Z                             # dt_hat_i/dw_j = z_ij  (the Jacobian is Z)

grad_by_chain_rule = jacobian.T @ (dL_de * de_dprediction)

print("Gradient by chain rule:", grad_by_chain_rule)
print("Gradient A w - b:      ", gradient(w))
print("Jacobian shape:", jacobian.shape, "(one row per house, one column per weight)")

Gradient by chain rule: [-3.1184 -2.7576]
Gradient A w - b:       [-3.1184 -2.7576]
Jacobian shape: (9858, 2) (one row per house, one column per weight)

3.3 Maxima / minima test at $w^*$¶

Second partial derivatives:

$$r = \frac{\partial^2 L}{\partial w_1^2} = 1, \qquad s = \frac{\partial^2 L}{\partial w_1 \partial w_2} = \rho, \qquad t = \frac{\partial^2 L}{\partial w_2^2} = 1$$

(These form the Hessian matrix $H = \begin{pmatrix} r & s\\ s & t\end{pmatrix} = A$.) If $rt - s^2 > 0$ and $r > 0$, the stationary point is a minimum.

In [16]:
# Module III: second derivatives, checked with finite differences of the gradient
r = A[0, 0]
s = A[0, 1]
t_second = A[1, 1]               # named t_second so it does not clash with the target t
rt_minus_s2 = r * t_second - s ** 2

r_numeric = (gradient(w_star + [h, 0])[0] - gradient(w_star - [h, 0])[0]) / (2 * h)
s_numeric = (gradient(w_star + [0, h])[0] - gradient(w_star - [0, h])[0]) / (2 * h)

print(f"Gradient at w*: {gradient(w_star)}  (zero => stationary point)")
print(f"r = {r:.4f} (numeric {r_numeric:.4f}),  s = {s:.4f} (numeric {s_numeric:.4f}),  t = {t_second:.4f}")
print(f"rt - s^2 = {rt_minus_s2:.4f}")
if rt_minus_s2 > 0 and r > 0:
    print("=> rt - s^2 > 0 and r > 0  =>  w* is a MINIMUM")

results["hessian_test"] = {"r": r, "s": s, "t": t_second, "rt_minus_s2": rt_minus_s2}

Gradient at w*: [0. 0.]  (zero => stationary point)
r = 1.0000 (numeric 1.0000),  s = 0.7777 (numeric 0.7777),  t = 1.0000
rt - s^2 = 0.3951
=> rt - s^2 > 0 and r > 0  =>  w* is a MINIMUM

3.4 Eigenvalues of the Hessian (characteristic equation)¶

$$\det(A - \lambda I) = \begin{vmatrix} 1-\lambda & \rho \\ \rho & 1-\lambda \end{vmatrix} = (1-\lambda)^2 - \rho^2 = 0 \quad\Rightarrow\quad \lambda = 1 \pm \rho$$

Eigenvectors: $\lambda_{\max} = 1 + \rho$ along $\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}(1, 1)$ (the steep direction), $\lambda_{\min} = 1 - \rho$ along $\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}(-1, 1)$ (the flat direction).

The condition number $\kappa = \lambda_{\max} / \lambda_{\min}$ measures how stretched the bowl is.

In [17]:
# Module I: characteristic equation  lambda^2 - (trace) lambda + det = 0, solved with the quadratic formula
trace_A = A[0, 0] + A[1, 1]
det_A = A[0, 0] * A[1, 1] - A[0, 1] * A[1, 0]
discriminant = trace_A ** 2 - 4 * det_A
lambda_min = (trace_A - np.sqrt(discriminant)) / 2
lambda_max = (trace_A + np.sqrt(discriminant)) / 2

print(f"Characteristic equation: lambda^2 - {trace_A:.4f} lambda + {det_A:.4f} = 0")
print(f"lambda_min = 1 - rho = {lambda_min:.4f}")
print(f"lambda_max = 1 + rho = {lambda_max:.4f}")

# Check with numpy (eigh returns eigenvalues in increasing order, eigenvectors as COLUMNS)
eigenvalues, P = np.linalg.eigh(A)
print("\nnumpy eigh check:  eigenvalues =", eigenvalues)

# An eigenvector times -1 is still an eigenvector. To keep signs fixed everywhere (notebook, slides,
# website) we flip each eigenvector so that its SECOND component is positive.
for col in range(2):
    if P[1, col] < 0:
        P[:, col] = -P[:, col]

print("eigenvector for lambda_min:", P[:, 0], "  = (-1, 1)/sqrt2  (flat direction)")
print("eigenvector for lambda_max:", P[:, 1], "  = ( 1, 1)/sqrt2  (steep direction)")
print("Check A v = lambda v:", np.allclose(A @ P, P * eigenvalues))

condition_number = lambda_max / lambda_min
print(f"\nCondition number kappa = {condition_number:.3f}")

results["eigenvalues"] = [lambda_min, lambda_max]
results["eigenvectors"] = [P[:, 0], P[:, 1]]       # one eigenvector per entry, same order as eigenvalues
results["condition_number"] = condition_number

lambda_min = 1 - rho = 0.2223
lambda_max = 1 + rho = 1.7777

numpy eigh check:  eigenvalues = [0.2223 1.7777]
eigenvector for lambda_min: [-0.7071  0.7071]   = (-1, 1)/sqrt2  (flat direction)
eigenvector for lambda_max: [0.7071 0.7071]   = ( 1, 1)/sqrt2  (steep direction)
Check A v = lambda v: True

3.5 What do the weights mean? (back to ₹)¶

Undo the standardisation: $\text{price} = \beta_0 + \beta_1\,\text{sqft} + \beta_2\,\text{bhk}$ with

$$\beta_1 = w_1 \frac{\sigma_{\text{price}}}{\sigma_{\text{sqft}}}, \qquad \beta_2 = w_2 \frac{\sigma_{\text{price}}}{\sigma_{\text{bhk}}}, \qquad \beta_0 = \overline{\text{price}} - \beta_1 \overline{\text{sqft}} - \beta_2 \overline{\text{bhk}}$$

Why is the BHK weight negative? Compare two flats of the same area: the one with more bedrooms has smaller rooms, and buyers pay slightly less for it. On its own, BHK is positively related to price (correlation 0.59) only because bigger flats have more bedrooms — once area is accounted for, the extra bedroom effect is slightly negative.

def loss_on_grid(W1, W2):
    """L(w1, w2) for whole grids at once, using the quadratic form L = ½ wᵀAw − b·w + ½·mean(t²)."""
    return (0.5 * (A[0, 0] * W1**2 + 2 * A[0, 1] * W1 * W2 + A[1, 1] * W2**2)
            - b[0] * W1 - b[1] * W2 + 0.5 * np.mean(t**2))

def draw_contours(ax, w1_range=(-2, 3), w2_range=(-2.5, 2), n_levels=14):
    """Contour lines of the loss, closer together near the minimum so the valley shape is visible."""
    W1, W2 = np.meshgrid(np.linspace(*w1_range, 300), np.linspace(*w2_range, 300))
    levels = loss_at_w_star + np.geomspace(0.003, 12, n_levels)
    ax.contour(W1, W2, loss_on_grid(W1, W2), levels=levels, cmap="viridis", linewidths=1)
    ax.plot(*w_star, marker="*", color=COLORS["red"], markersize=18, markeredgecolor="black",
            linestyle="none", label="minimum w*", zorder=5)
    ax.set_xlim(w1_range)
    ax.set_ylim(w2_range)
    ax.set_aspect("equal")
    ax.set_xlabel("$w_1$ (sqft weight)")
    ax.set_ylabel("$w_2$ (bhk weight)")

Part 4 — Constrained training: Lagrange multipliers¶

Syllabus link: Module III — Lagrange's method of undetermined multipliers (CO3)

What we compute: the best weights when the total "weight budget" is limited: minimise $L(w)$ subject to $w_1^2 + w_2^2 = s^2$ with $s = 0.6$ (smaller than $\|w^*\| \approx 0.977$, so the unconstrained minimum is not allowed).

Key result: $\mu = 0.2879$, $w_c = (0.5913,\ 0.1018)$, $L(w_c) = 0.1696$. At $w_c$ the gradient is parallel to $w_c$ — the loss contour just touches the circle.

4.1 The Lagrange function¶

$$F(w_1, w_2, \mu) = L(w) + \frac{\mu}{2}\left(w_1^2 + w_2^2 - s^2\right)$$

Setting $\partial F/\partial w_1 = \partial F/\partial w_2 = 0$:

$$\nabla L + \mu\, w = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; A w - b + \mu w = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; (A + \mu I)\, w = b$$

For each value of $\mu$ this is a $2\times2$ linear system (solved by our Gauss elimination). We then choose $\mu$ so that the solution lies exactly on the circle: $\|w(\mu)\| = s$ (root-finding).

In [23]:
from scipy.optimize import brentq    # scipy is used only to find the root mu

s_budget = 0.6                       # radius of the constraint circle
print(f"||w*|| = {np.linalg.norm(w_star):.4f}  >  s = {s_budget}  -> constraint is active")

def w_of_mu(mu):
    """Module III: solve (A + mu I) w = b with our own Gauss elimination."""
    _, w = gauss_elimination(A + mu * np.eye(2), b)
    return w

def distance_from_circle(mu):
    return np.linalg.norm(w_of_mu(mu)) - s_budget

# ||w(mu)|| shrinks as mu grows: positive at mu = 0, negative at mu = 10, so the root is in between
mu = brentq(distance_from_circle, 0.0, 10.0, xtol=1e-12)
w_c = w_of_mu(mu)
loss_c = loss(w_c)

print(f"mu   = {mu:.4f}")
print(f"w_c  = ({w_c[0]:.4f}, {w_c[1]:.4f}),   ||w_c|| = {np.linalg.norm(w_c):.4f}")
print(f"L(w_c) = {loss_c:.4f}   (compare unconstrained L(w*) = {loss_at_w_star:.4f})")

||w*|| = 0.9775  >  s = 0.6  -> constraint is active
mu   = 0.2879
w_c  = (0.5913, 0.1018),   ||w_c|| = 0.6000
L(w_c) = 0.1696   (compare unconstrained L(w*) = 0.1416)

4.2 Check tangency: $\nabla L(w_c)$ is parallel to $w_c$¶

From $\nabla L + \mu w = 0$, each component of $\nabla L(w_c)$ divided by the same component of $w_c$ should equal $-\mu$.

In one line: adding a penalty $\frac{\mu}{2}\|w\|^2$ to the loss is called ridge regression — a standard regularisation method used in AI to stop weights from growing too large.

Part 5 — Training as a differential equation¶

Syllabus link: Module II — systems of first-order linear ODEs, solution by diagonalisation, stability; total derivative (Module III); Euler's method (CO2)

What we compute: the exact path the weights follow if we train with infinitely small steps (gradient flow), and show that ordinary gradient descent is just Euler's method on that ODE.

Key result: $z_i(t) = z_i(0)\,e^{-\lambda_i t}$ — two exponential decays with time constants $1/\lambda = 4.4994$ (slow) and $0.5625$ (fast). Gradient descent $w_{k+1} = w_k - \eta \nabla L$ = Euler's method with step $h = \eta$.

5.1 Gradient flow ODE¶

Gradient descent moves the weights downhill: $w_{k+1} = w_k - \eta\,\nabla L(w_k)$. With very small steps this becomes a system of first-order linear ODEs:

$$\frac{dw}{dt} = -\nabla L(w) = -(A w - b) = -A\,(w - w^*) \qquad (\text{since } A w^* = b)$$

Solve by diagonalisation. Let $u = w - w^*$ and $A = P D P^{\mathsf T}$ ($P$ = eigenvectors, $D$ = eigenvalues). With $z = P^{\mathsf T} u$ the system uncouples:

$$z_i' = -\lambda_i z_i \quad\Rightarrow\quad z_i(t) = z_i(0)\, e^{-\lambda_i t}$$

$$\boxed{\,w(t) = w^* + P \begin{pmatrix} e^{-\lambda_1 t} & 0 \\ 0 & e^{-\lambda_2 t}\end{pmatrix} P^{\mathsf T} (w_0 - w^*)\,}$$

Starting point for all training runs: $w_0 = (-1.5,\ -1.0)$.

In [26]:
w0 = np.array([-1.5, -1.0])
D = np.diag(eigenvalues)
print("Diagonalisation check, P D P^T = A:", np.allclose(P @ D @ P.T, A))

u0 = w0 - w_star
z0 = P.T @ u0                         # eigen-coordinates of the starting error
print(f"w0 - w* = {u0}")
print(f"eigen-coordinates z(0) = P^T (w0 - w*) = ({z0[0]:.4f}, {z0[1]:.4f})"
      f"   [slow mode lambda={lambda_min:.4f}, fast mode lambda={lambda_max:.4f}]")

def w_exact(time):
    """Module II: closed-form solution of the gradient-flow ODE at time t."""
    z_t = z0 * np.exp(-eigenvalues * time)       # each mode decays on its own
    return w_star + P @ z_t

# Check that w_exact really solves w' = -A (w - w*): compare a numerical derivative with the right-hand side
for time in [0.0, 1.0, 5.0]:
    dw_dt_numeric = (w_exact(time + 1e-6) - w_exact(time - 1e-6)) / 2e-6
    print(f"t = {time}:  w'(t) numeric = {dw_dt_numeric},  -A(w - w*) = {-A @ (w_exact(time) - w_star)}")

results["w0"] = w0
results["eigen_coords_w0"] = z0

5.2 Stability¶

The ODE $u' = -A u$ has coefficient matrix $-A$ with eigenvalues $-\lambda_{\min}, -\lambda_{\max}$ — both negative, so $u(t) \to 0$ from any start: an asymptotically stable node. Each mode has a time constant $\tau_i = 1/\lambda_i$ (time to shrink by a factor $e$): the steep direction settles fast, the flat direction slowly.

In [27]:

      f"  fast mode 1/lambda_max = {time_constants[1]:.4f}")

5.3 Total derivative: the loss never goes up¶

Along the flow, by the chain rule for a function of two variables:

$$\frac{dL}{dt} = \frac{\partial L}{\partial w_1}\frac{dw_1}{dt} + \frac{\partial L}{\partial w_2}\frac{dw_2}{dt} = \nabla L \cdot w' = -\|\nabla L\|^2 \le 0$$

In [28]:
print(" t    dL/dt (numeric)   -||grad L||^2")
for time in [0.0, 0.5, 1.0, 2.0, 5.0, 10.0]:
    dL_dt_numeric = (loss(w_exact(time + 1e-6)) - loss(w_exact(time - 1e-6))) / 2e-6
    formula = -np.sum(gradient(w_exact(time)) ** 2)
    print(f"{time:4.1f}   {dL_dt_numeric:14.6f}   {formula:14.6f}")

5.4 Gradient descent = Euler's method¶

Euler's method for $w' = f(w)$ with step $h$ is $w_{k+1} = w_k + h\, f(w_k)$. With $f(w) = -\nabla L(w)$:

$$w_{k+1} = w_k - h\,\nabla L(w_k)$$

— exactly gradient descent with learning rate $\eta = h$. After $k$ steps, gradient descent should be close to the exact ODE solution at time $t = k\eta$ when $\eta$ is small, and drift away when $\eta$ is large.

In [29]:
def gradient_descent(eta, n_steps, start=w0):
    """Module II: Euler's method on w' = -grad L  (= gradient descent with learning rate eta)."""
    path = [np.array(start, dtype=float)]
    for _ in range(n_steps):
        w = path[-1]
        path.append(w - eta * gradient(w))         # w_{k+1} = w_k - eta * grad L(w_k)
    return np.array(path)

for eta, n_steps in [(0.1, 100), (1.0, 10)]:
    path = gradient_descent(eta, n_steps)
    exact_points = np.array([w_exact(k * eta) for k in range(n_steps + 1)])
    max_gap = np.max(np.abs(path - exact_points))
    print(f"eta = {eta}: largest gap between GD and exact ODE solution over t in [0, 10] = {max_gap:.4f}")

eta = 0.1: largest gap between GD and exact ODE solution over t in [0, 10] = 0.0593
eta = 1.0: largest gap between GD and exact ODE solution over t in [0, 10] = 1.5833

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(15, 7))
for i, ax in enumerate(axes):
    ax.plot(times, exact_path[:, i], color=COLORS["black"], lw=2.5, label="exact ODE solution")

                label=f"gradient descent η = {eta}  (t = kη)")
    ax.axhline(w_star[i], color=COLORS["red"], linestyle=":", lw=2, label="minimum w* (where training ends)")
    # label placed in a gap between the orange squares

5.5 Optional extension: momentum = a damped oscillator (second-order ODE)¶

Momentum gradient descent adds "velocity" to the weights. In the continuous limit, each eigen-direction obeys

$$z'' + \gamma\, z' + \lambda\, z = 0$$

Auxiliary (characteristic) equation $m^2 + \gamma m + \lambda = 0 \Rightarrow m = \frac{-\gamma \pm \sqrt{\gamma^2 - 4\lambda}}{2}$:

  • $\gamma^2 < 4\lambda$: complex roots → under-damped (oscillates while decaying)
  • $\gamma^2 = 4\lambda$: equal roots → critically damped (fastest without oscillating), $\gamma = 2\sqrt\lambda$
  • $\gamma^2 > 4\lambda$: distinct real roots → over-damped (slow, no oscillation)
In [32]:
momentum_critical_gamma = 2 * np.sqrt(eigenvalues)
print(f"Critical damping gamma = 2 sqrt(lambda):  slow mode {momentum_critical_gamma[0]:.4f},"
      f"  fast mode {momentum_critical_gamma[1]:.4f}")

def damped_solution(gamma, lam, time, z_start=1.0):
    """Module II: solution of z'' + gamma z' + lam z = 0 with z(0) = z_start, z'(0) = 0."""
    disc = gamma ** 2 - 4 * lam
    if disc > 1e-12:                                   # over-damped: two real roots
        m1 = (-gamma + np.sqrt(disc)) / 2
        m2 = (-gamma - np.sqrt(disc)) / 2
        c1, c2 = m2 / (m2 - m1), -m1 / (m2 - m1)
        return z_start * (c1 * np.exp(m1 * time) + c2 * np.exp(m2 * time))
    if disc < -1e-12:                                  # under-damped: complex roots alpha ± i beta
        alpha, beta = -gamma / 2, np.sqrt(-disc) / 2
        return z_start * np.exp(alpha * time) * (np.cos(beta * time) - alpha / beta * np.sin(beta * time))
    m = -gamma / 2                                     # critically damped: repeated root
    return z_start * (1 - m * time) * np.exp(m * time)

# Three cases for the slow mode lambda_min (starting from its eigen-coordinate z(0))
damping_cases = {"under-damped": 0.3, "critically damped": momentum_critical_gamma[0], "over-damped": 2.5}
momentum_times = np.linspace(0, 30, 600)
momentum_curves = {name: damped_solution(gamma, lambda_min, momentum_times, z0[0])
                   for name, gamma in damping_cases.items()}

# Cross-check the closed forms with scipy's numerical ODE solver
from scipy.integrate import solve_ivp
for name, gamma in damping_cases.items():
    numeric = solve_ivp(lambda _, y: [y[1], -gamma * y[1] - lambda_min * y[0]], (0, 30), [z0[0], 0.0],
                        t_eval=momentum_times, rtol=1e-10, atol=1e-12).y[0]
    print(f"{name:18s} gamma = {gamma:.4f}: max difference from scipy = {np.max(np.abs(numeric - momentum_curves[name])):.1e}")

results["momentum_critical_gamma"] = momentum_critical_gamma

Part 6 — The learning-rate limit¶

Syllabus link: Modules I + II combined — eigenvalues and diagonalisation decide the stability of the discrete (Euler) training process (CO6)

What we compute: the largest learning rate for which training converges, predicted from the eigenvalues before training — then we train with 7 learning rates and check the prediction.

Key result: $\eta_{\text{crit}} = 2/\lambda_{\max} = 1.125$. Training with $\eta = 1.12$ converges, $\eta = 1.13$ explodes — the maths predicts the AI's behaviour.

6.1 Gradient descent in eigen-coordinates¶

With $u_k = w_k - w^*$: $\;u_{k+1} = u_k - \eta A u_k = (I - \eta A)\,u_k$. In eigen-coordinates $z = P^{\mathsf T} u$ the matrix is diagonal, so each mode is multiplied by its own factor every step:

$$z_i \;\leftarrow\; (1 - \eta \lambda_i)\, z_i \qquad\Rightarrow\qquad z_i^{(k)} = (1 - \eta\lambda_i)^k\, z_i^{(0)}$$

Training converges if and only if $|1 - \eta\lambda_i| < 1$ for every $i$:

$$-1 < 1 - \eta\lambda_i < 1 \iff 0 < \eta < \frac{2}{\lambda_i} \quad\text{for all } i \iff \boxed{0 < \eta < \frac{2}{\lambda_{\max}} = \eta_{\text{crit}}}$$

  • Factor between 0 and 1: smooth convergence. Factor between −1 and 0: zig-zag convergence.
  • Factor beyond −1: each step overshoots further → explodes.

The best (optimal) rate makes the two modes shrink equally fast: $1 - \eta\lambda_{\min} = -(1 - \eta\lambda_{\max})$

$$\eta_{\text{opt}} = \frac{2}{\lambda_{\max} + \lambda_{\min}} = \frac{2}{2} = 1, \qquad \text{factor at } \eta_{\text{opt}} = \frac{\kappa - 1}{\kappa + 1} = \rho$$

In [34]:
eta_crit = 2 / lambda_max
eta_opt = 2 / (lambda_max + lambda_min)

def stability_factor(eta):
    """Largest |1 - eta * lambda_i|: the error shrinks (or grows) by at most this much per step."""
    return np.max(np.abs(1 - eta * eigenvalues))

print(f"eta_crit = 2 / lambda_max = {eta_crit:.4f}")
print(f"eta_opt  = 2 / (lambda_max + lambda_min) = {eta_opt:.4f}")
print(f"factor at eta_opt = {stability_factor(eta_opt):.4f};  (kappa-1)/(kappa+1) = "
      f"{(condition_number - 1) / (condition_number + 1):.4f};  rho = {rho:.4f}")

6.2 Train with 7 learning rates¶

Start at $w_0 = (-1.5, -1.0)$. Stop when $\|w - w^*\| < 10^{-6}$ (converged) or $\|w\| > 10^{6}$ (exploded), at most 2,000 steps.

In [35]:
LEARNING_RATES = [0.1, 0.5, 1.0, 1.10, 1.12, 1.13, 1.15]

def train(eta, start=w0, tol=1e-6, blow_up=1e6, max_steps=2000):
    """Hand-written gradient descent with stopping rules. Returns (outcome, steps, path)."""
    w = np.array(start, dtype=float)
    path = [w.copy()]
    for step in range(1, max_steps + 1):
        w = w - eta * gradient(w)                  # one gradient-descent (Euler) step
        path.append(w.copy())
        if np.linalg.norm(w - w_star) < tol:
            return "converged", step, np.array(path)
        if np.linalg.norm(w) > blow_up:
            return "exploded", step, np.array(path)
    return "not finished", max_steps, np.array(path)

gd_runs = []
gd_paths = {}
for eta in LEARNING_RATES:
    outcome, steps, path = train(eta)
    gd_paths[eta] = path
    gd_runs.append({"eta": eta, "factor": stability_factor(eta), "outcome": outcome, "steps": steps})

gd_table = pd.DataFrame(gd_runs)
gd_table["predicted"] = np.where(gd_table["factor"] < 1, "converge", "explode")
gd_table.round(4)

        on_screen = view_w1[0] <= current[0] <= view_w1[1] and view_w2[0] <= current[1] <= view_w2[1]
        dots[i].set_data([current[0]], [current[1]])
        dots[i].set_visible(on_screen)
        trails[i].set_visible(on_screen)
        banners[i].set_text("" if on_screen else "weights flew off the chart!")
        banners[i].set_visible(not on_screen)
        labels[i].set_text(f"step {step}\n‖w − w*‖ = {np.linalg.norm(current - w_star):.3g}")
        distances = np.linalg.norm(path[:step + 1] - w_star, axis=1)
        distance_lines[i].set_data(np.arange(step + 1), distances)
    fig.canvas.draw()
    frames.append(Image.fromarray(np.asarray(fig.canvas.buffer_rgba())[:, :, :3]))
plt.close(fig)

durations = [180] * (len(frames) - 1) + [2000]        # hold the last frame for 2 seconds
frames[0].save(FIGURES / "anim_converge_vs_explode.gif", save_all=True, append_images=frames[1:],
               duration=durations, loop=0)
print(f"Saved anim_converge_vs_explode.gif ({len(frames)} frames)")

Appendix — How the clean data set was made (for the report)¶

The analysis above uses the provided bangalore_houses_clean.csv. This appendix re-creates it from the raw Kaggle file to document every cleaning step. It does not change anything used above.

In [42]:
raw = pd.read_csv(PROJECT_ROOT / "data" / "Bengaluru_House_Data_raw.csv")
cleaning_log = [("Raw", len(raw))]

def parse_sqft(text):
    """'1200' -> 1200;  '1000 - 1400' -> 1200 (midpoint);  '34.46Sq. Meter' etc. -> NaN (dropped)."""
    text = str(text).strip()
    try:
        if " - " in text:
            low, high = text.split(" - ")
            return (float(low) + float(high)) / 2
        return float(text)
    except ValueError:
        return np.nan

step = raw.dropna(subset=["size", "total_sqft", "price"]).copy()
cleaning_log.append(("Drop missing size / sqft / price", len(step)))

step["sqft"] = step["total_sqft"].map(parse_sqft)
step = step.dropna(subset=["sqft"])
cleaning_log.append(("Drop non-numeric sqft; ranges -> midpoint", len(step)))

step = step[~step["area_type"].str.contains("Plot")]       # plot prices include the land
cleaning_log.append(('Drop "Plot Area" listings', len(step)))

step["bhk"] = step["size"].str.extract(r"(\d+)")[0].astype(int)
step = step[step["bhk"].between(1, 5)]
cleaning_log.append(("Keep 1-5 BHK", len(step)))

step = step[step["sqft"] / step["bhk"] >= 300]
cleaning_log.append(("Drop < 300 sqft per bedroom", len(step)))

price_per_sqft = step["price"] * 1e5 / step["sqft"]
low, high = price_per_sqft.quantile([0.01, 0.99])
step = step[price_per_sqft.between(low, high)]
cleaning_log.append((f"Price per sqft within 1st-99th percentile (₹{low:,.0f}-{high:,.0f})", len(step)))

low, high = step["sqft"].quantile([0.005, 0.995])
step = step[step["sqft"].between(low, high)]
cleaning_log.append((f"sqft within 0.5-99.5 percentile ({low:,.0f}-{high:,.0f})", len(step)))

step = step.drop_duplicates(subset=["location", "sqft", "bhk", "price"])
cleaning_log.append(("Drop duplicate listings", len(step)))

reproduced = step.rename(columns={"price": "price_lakhs"})[["location", "area_type", "sqft", "bhk", "price_lakhs"]]
same_as_provided = (np.allclose(np.sort(reproduced["sqft"].round(1)), np.sort(houses["sqft"]))
                    and np.allclose(np.sort(reproduced["price_lakhs"]), np.sort(houses["price_lakhs"])))
print("Reproduced file matches the provided clean file (sqft rounded to 1 d.p.):", same_as_provided)
pd.DataFrame(cleaning_log, columns=["Step", "Rows left"])

Headline result: the eigenvalues predicted the boundary $\eta_{\text{crit}} = 1.125$ before we trained. With $\eta = 1.12$ (factor 0.991) the model learns — slowly, zig-zagging; with $\eta = 1.13$ (factor 1.009) the error grows by 0.9% every step and the weights explode. The maths predicts the AI's behaviour.

In [44]:
def to_plain(value):
    """Convert numpy types to plain Python so json can save them."""
    if isinstance(value, dict):
        return {k: to_plain(v) for k, v in value.items()}
    if isinstance(value, (list, tuple, np.ndarray)):
        return [to_plain(v) for v in value]
    if isinstance(value, np.integer):
        return int(value)
    if isinstance(value, np.floating):
        return float(value)
    return value

RESULTS_FILE.write_text(json.dumps(to_plain(results), indent=2), encoding="utf-8")
print(f"Saved {len(results)} keys to {RESULTS_FILE.name}")
